danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 21
paragraphs: Pierre kørte hen til Marja Dmitrijevna for at meddele hende, at hendes ønske om at forvise Kuragin fra Moskva var opfyldt. Hele huset var i alarm og forvirring. Natasja var meget syg; som Marja Dmitrijevna fortalte ham i fortrolighed, havde hun forgiftet sig selv natten efter, at hun havde fået at vide, at Anatole var gift, med noget arsenik, hun i hemmelighed havde skaffet sig. Efter at have slugt en smule var hun blevet så forskrækket, at hun vækkede Sonja og fortalte hende, hvad hun havde gjort. De nødvendige modgifte var blevet givet i tide, og hun var nu uden for fare, men dog stadig så svag, at det var udelukket at flytte hende til landet, og grevinden var derfor blevet tilkaldt. Pierre så den ulykkelige greve og Sonja med tårevædet ansigt, men han kunne ikke se Natasja.

Pierre spiste til middag i Klubben den dag og hørte fra alle sider sladder om det forsøgte bortførsel af Rostova. Han benægtede rygterne beslutsomt og forsikrede alle om, at der ikke var sket andet, end at hans svoger havde friet til hende og fået afslag. Det forekom Pierre, at det var hans pligt at skjule hele affæren og genoprette Natasjas ry.
Han ventede fyrst Andrejs hjemkomst med frygt og kørte hver dag til den gamle fyrste for at få nyt om ham.

Den gamle fyrst Bolkonskij havde hørt alle de rygter, der cirkulerede i byen, fra Mademoiselle Bourienne og havde læst den seddel til fyrstinde Marja, hvori Natasja havde brudt forlovelsen. Han virkede i bedre humør end sædvanligt og ventede sin søn med stor utålmodighed.
Nogle dage efter Anatoles afrejse modtog Pierre en seddel fra fyrst Andrej, der meddelte sin ankomst og bad ham komme og besøge ham.

Så snart fyrst Andrej var kommet til Moskva, havde han fra sin far modtaget Natasjas seddel til fyrstinde Marja, hvori hun brød forlovelsen (Mademoiselle Bourienne havde stjålet den fra fyrstinde Marja og givet den til den gamle fyrste), og han hørte fra ham historien om Natasjas bortførelseforsøg, med tildigtninger.

Fyrst Andrej var ankommet om aftenen, og Pierre kom for at besøge ham næste morgen. Pierre forventede at finde fyrst Andrej i næsten samme tilstand som Natasja og blev derfor overrasket over, da han trådte ind i salonen, at høre ham i arbejdsværelset tale med høj, livlig stemme om en eller anden intrige i Petersborg. Den gamle fyrstes stemme og en andens afbrød ham nu og da. Fyrstinde Marja kom ud for at møde Pierre. Hun sukkede og så hen mod døren til det rum, hvor fyrst Andrej var, tydeligvis med den hensigt at udtrykke sin medfølelse med hans sorg, men Pierre kunne se på hendes ansigt, at hun var glad både over, hvad der var sket, og over den måde, hendes bror havde taget nyheden om Natasjas troløshed.

»Han siger, han ventede det,« bemærkede hun. »Jeg ved, hans stolthed ikke vil tillade ham at udtrykke sine følelser, men alligevel har han taget det bedre, langt bedre end jeg ventede. Det skulle tydeligvis ske sådan...«
»Men er det virkelig muligt, at alt er helt forbi?« spurgte Pierre.

Fyrstinde Marja så forbavset på ham. Hun forstod ikke, hvordan han kunne stille et sådant spørgsmål. Pierre gik ind i arbejdsværelset. Fyrst Andrej, meget forandret og tydeligvis ved bedre helbred, men med en ny vandrette rynke mellem brynene, stod i civil påklædning over for sin far og fyrst Mesjtjerskij og diskuterede ivrigt og gestikulerede heftigt. Samtalen drejede sig om Speranskij — nyheden om hvis pludselige forvisning og påståede forræderi netop var nået til Moskva.

»Nu dadler og anklager alle dem ham, som for en måned siden var begejstrede for ham,« sagde fyrst Andrej, »og de, der var ude af stand til at forstå hans mål. At dømme en mand i unåde og lægge al skyld for andres fejl på ham er meget let, men jeg fastholder, at hvis noget godt er udrettet under denne regering, er det gjort af ham, af ham alene.«
Han standsede ved synet af Pierre. Hans ansigt dirrede og antog straks et hævngerrigt udtryk.
»Eftertiden vil yde ham retfærdighed,« sluttede han og vendte sig straks mod Pierre.
»Nå, hvordan har du det? Bliver stadig tykkere?« sagde han livligt, men den nye rynke i hans pande blev dybere. »Ja, jeg har det godt,« sagde han som svar på Pierres spørgsmål og smilede.
For Pierre sagde det smil tydeligt: »Jeg har det godt, men mit helbred er nu ikke til nytte for nogen.«

Efter nogle ord til Pierre om de forfærdelige veje fra den polske grænse, om folk, han havde mødt i Schweiz og som kendte Pierre, og om monsieur Dessalles, som han havde bragt med fra udlandet som sin søns huslærer, deltog fyrst Andrej igen varmt i samtalen om Speranskij, der stadig stod på mellem de to gamle mænd.

»Hvis der var forræderi, eller beviser for hemmelige forbindelser med Napoleon, ville de være blevet offentliggjort,« sagde han med varme og hast. »Jeg kan ikke lide og har aldrig kunnet lide Speranskij personligt, men jeg holder af retfærdighed!«

Pierre genkendte nu i sin ven et behov, han kendte alt for godt, for at ophidse sig og diskutere uvedkommende emner for at kvæle tanker, der var alt for trykkende og alt for intime. Da fyrst Mesjtjerskij var gået, tog fyrst Andrej Pierre under armen og bad ham ind i det værelse, der var tildelt ham. Der var redt en seng, og der stod nogle åbne kufferter og rejsetasker. Fyrst Andrej gik hen til en af dem og tog en lille æske frem, hvorfra han trak en pakke svøbt i papir. Han gjorde det hele tavst og meget hurtigt. Han rejste sig og hostede. Hans ansigt var mørkt, og hans læber var sammenpressede.
»Tilgiv, at jeg besværer dig...«

Pierre så, at fyrst Andrej var i færd med at tale om Natasja, og hans brede ansigt udtrykte medlidenhed og medfølelse. Dette udtryk irriterede fyrst Andrej, og med en bestemt, ringende og ubehagelig tone fortsatte han:
»Jeg har modtaget et afslag fra grevinde Rostova og har hørt rygter om, at din svoger har friet til hende, eller noget i den retning. Er det sandt?«
»Både sandt og usandt,« begyndte Pierre; men fyrst Andrej afbrød ham.
»Her er hendes breve og hendes portræt,« sagde han.
Han tog pakken fra bordet og rakte den til Pierre.
»Giv dette til grevinden... hvis du ser hende.«
»Hun er meget syg,« sagde Pierre.
»Så hun er stadig her?« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Og fyrst Kuragin?« tilføjede han hurtigt.
»Han rejste for længe siden. Hun har svævet mellem liv og død.«
»Jeg beklager hendes sygdom meget,« sagde fyrst Andrej; og han smilede som sin far, koldt, ondsindet og ubehageligt.
»Så monsieur Kuragin har ikke beæret grevinde Rostova med sin hånd?« sagde fyrst Andrej, og han fnøs flere gange.
»Han kunne ikke gifte sig, for han var allerede gift,« sagde Pierre.
Fyrst Andrej lo ubehageligt og mindede igen om sin far.
»Og hvor er din svoger nu, om jeg må spørge?« sagde han.
»Han er taget til Peters... Men det ved jeg ikke,« sagde Pierre.
»Nå, det er ligegyldigt,« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Sig grevinde Rostova, at hun var og er fuldstændig fri, og at jeg ønsker hende alt godt.«
Pierre tog pakken. Fyrst Andrej, som om han forsøgte at huske, om han havde mere at sige, eller ventede på, om Pierre ville sige noget, stirrede fast på ham.
»Sig mig, husker du vores diskussion i Petersborg?« spurgte Pierre, »om...«
»Ja,« svarede fyrst Andrej hurtigt. »Jeg sagde, at en falden kvinde bør tilgives, men jeg sagde ikke, at jeg kunne tilgive hende. Det kan jeg ikke.«
»Men kan dette sammenlignes...?« sagde Pierre.

Fyrst Andrej afbrød ham og udbrød skarpt: »Ja, fri til hende igen, vær storsindet og så videre?... Ja, det ville være meget ædelt, men jeg er ude af stand til at følge i den herres fodspor. Hvis du ønsker at være min ven, så tal aldrig mere til mig om det... om alt det! Nå, farvel. Så du giver hende pakken?«
Pierre forlod rummet og gik hen til den gamle fyrste og fyrstinde Marja.

Den gamle mand virkede livligere end sædvanligt. Fyrstinde Marja var den samme som altid, men under hendes medfølelse med broderen bemærkede Pierre hendes tilfredshed med, at forlovelsen var blevet brudt. Da han så på dem, indså Pierre, hvilken foragt og fjendtlighed de alle følte for familien Rostov, og at det i deres nærværelse var umuligt så meget som at nævne navnet på hende, der kunne opgive fyrst Andrej for en hvilken som helst anden.

Til middag drejede samtalen sig om krigen, hvis tilnærmelse blev stadig tydeligere. Fyrst Andrej talte uafbrudt og argumenterede snart med sin far, snart med den schweiziske huslærer Dessalles, og udviste en unaturlig livlighed, hvis årsag Pierre så godt forstod.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 21
paragraphs: Pierre drove to Marya Dmitrievna's to tell her that her wish had been fulfilled and Kuragin had been banished from Moscow. The whole house was in a state of alarm and commotion. Natasha was very ill, having — as Marya Dmitrievna told him in secret — poisoned herself the night after she was told Anatole was married, with some arsenic she had secretly obtained. After swallowing a little she had been so frightened that she woke Sonya and told her what she had done. The necessary antidotes had been given in time and she was now out of danger, though still so weak that it was out of the question to move her to the country, and so the countess had been sent for. Pierre saw the distracted count and Sonya's tear-stained face, but couldn't see Natasha.

Pierre dined at the Club that day and heard gossip on all sides about the attempted abduction of Rostova. He firmly denied these rumors, assuring everyone that nothing had happened except that his brother-in-law had proposed to her and been refused. It seemed to Pierre that it was his duty to cover up the whole affair and restore Natasha's reputation.
He was dreading Prince Andrew's return and went every day to the old prince's house for news of him.

Old Prince Bolkonsky had heard all the rumors circulating in the town from Mademoiselle Bourienne and had read the note to Princess Mary in which Natasha had broken off her engagement. He seemed in better spirits than usual and awaited his son with great impatience.
Some days after Anatole's departure, Pierre received a note from Prince Andrew informing him of his arrival and asking him to come and see him.

As soon as he reached Moscow, Prince Andrew had received from his father Natasha's note to Princess Mary breaking off her engagement (Mademoiselle Bourienne had stolen it from Princess Mary and given it to the old prince), and he heard from his father the story of Natasha's elopement attempt, with additions.

Prince Andrew had arrived in the evening, and Pierre came to see him the next morning. Pierre expected to find Prince Andrew in almost the same state as Natasha and was therefore surprised on entering the drawing room to hear him in the study talking loudly and animatedly about some intrigue in Petersburg. The old prince's voice and another occasionally interrupted him. Princess Mary came out to meet Pierre. She sighed, looking toward the door of the room where Prince Andrew was, clearly wanting to express her sympathy with his sorrow, but Pierre saw by her face that she was glad both at what had happened and at the way her brother had taken the news of Natasha's faithlessness.
"He says he expected it," she remarked. "I know his pride won't let him express his feelings, but still he has taken it better, far better, than I expected. Evidently it had to be..."
"But is it possible that it's really all over?" asked Pierre.

Princess Mary looked at him with astonishment. She couldn't understand how he could ask such a question. Pierre went into the study. Prince Andrew, greatly changed and clearly in better health, but with a fresh horizontal wrinkle between his brows, stood in civilian clothes facing his father and Prince Meshchersky, arguing heatedly and gesticulating vigorously. The conversation was about Speransky — the news of whose sudden exile and alleged treachery had just reached Moscow.

"Now he is condemned and blamed by everyone who was enthusiastic about him a month ago," Prince Andrew was saying, "and by those who were unable to understand his aims. To judge a man who is in disgrace and blame him for other men's mistakes is very easy, but I maintain that if anything good has been accomplished in this reign, it was done by him — by him alone."
He paused at the sight of Pierre. His face quivered and immediately assumed a vindictive expression.
"Posterity will do him justice," he concluded, and at once turned to Pierre.
"Well, how are you? Still getting stouter?" he said with energy, but the new wrinkle on his forehead deepened. "Yes, I am well," he said in answer to Pierre's question, and smiled.
To Pierre, that smile clearly said: "I am well, but my health is of no use to anyone now."

After a few words to Pierre about the awful roads from the Polish border, about people he had met in Switzerland who knew Pierre, and about Monsieur Dessalles, whom he had brought from abroad to be his son's tutor, Prince Andrew again joined warmly in the conversation about Speransky that was still going on between the two old men.

"If there were treason, or evidence of secret dealings with Napoleon, they would have been made public," he said with heat and haste. "I do not, and never did, like Speransky personally, but I like justice!"

Pierre now recognized in his friend a need he knew only too well — to get worked up and argue about unrelated matters in order to stifle thoughts that were too painful and too intimate. When Prince Meshchersky had left, Prince Andrew took Pierre's arm and asked him into the room assigned to him. A bed had been made up there, and some open trunks and bags stood about. Prince Andrew went to one and took out a small casket, from which he drew a packet wrapped in paper. He did it all silently and very quickly. He stood up and coughed. His face was gloomy and his lips compressed.
"Forgive me for troubling you..."

Pierre saw that Prince Andrew was going to speak of Natasha, and his broad face expressed pity and sympathy. This expression irritated Prince Andrew, and in a determined, ringing, and unpleasant tone he continued:
"I have received a refusal from Countess Rostova, and have heard reports of your brother-in-law having sought her hand, or something of that kind. Is that true?"
"Both true and untrue," Pierre began; but Prince Andrew interrupted him.
"Here are her letters and her portrait," said he.
He took the packet from the table and handed it to Pierre.
"Give this to the countess... if you see her."
"She is very ill," said Pierre.
"Then she is still here?" said Prince Andrew. "And Prince Kuragin?" he added quickly.
"He left long ago. She has been at death's door."
"I deeply regret her illness," said Prince Andrew; and he smiled like his father — coldly, maliciously, and unpleasantly.
"So Monsieur Kuragin has not honored Countess Rostova with his hand?" said Prince Andrew, and he snorted several times.
"He couldn't marry — he was already married," said Pierre.
Prince Andrew laughed disagreeably, again reminding one of his father.
"And where is your brother-in-law now, if I may ask?" he said.
"He has gone to Peters... But I don't know," said Pierre.
"Well, it doesn't matter," said Prince Andrew. "Tell Countess Rostova that she was and is perfectly free and that I wish her all that is good."
Pierre took the packet. Prince Andrew, as if trying to remember whether he had something more to say, or waiting to see if Pierre would speak, looked steadily at him.
"I say, do you remember our discussion in Petersburg?" asked Pierre, "about..."
"Yes," returned Prince Andrew hastily. "I said that a fallen woman should be forgiven, but I didn't say I could forgive her. I can't."
"But can this be compared...?" said Pierre.

Prince Andrew interrupted him and cried sharply: "Yes, ask for her hand again, be magnanimous, and so on?... Yes, that would be very noble, but I am unable to follow in that gentleman's footsteps. If you wish to be my friend, never speak to me of that... of all that! Well, goodbye. So you'll give her the packet?"
Pierre left the room and went to the old prince and Princess Mary.

The old man seemed livelier than usual. Princess Mary was the same as always, but beneath her sympathy for her brother, Pierre detected her satisfaction that the engagement had been broken off. Looking at them, Pierre realized what contempt and hostility they all felt toward the Rostovs, and that it was impossible in their presence even to mention the name of the woman who could give up Prince Andrew for anyone else.

At dinner the conversation turned to the war, the approach of which was becoming obvious. Prince Andrew talked constantly, arguing now with his father, now with the Swiss tutor Dessalles, and showing an unnatural animation whose cause Pierre understood only too well.
